To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
we have developed a geostatistical model for estimating treatment burdens of presumed malaria in Kenya that can be used for any level of spatial aggregation.
we have shown that geostatistical modelling can be used to improve the quality of data from health management information systems in Africa.

a space–time geostatistical modelling approach can be applied to incomplete health management information systems data to produce reliable and timely estimates of treatment burden at national and subnational scales.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of a geostatistical approach to improve health management information systems in Africa.
improving the quality of health data for the planning and management of national health systems in Africa.
the problem of incomplete data in health management information systems (HIMS).
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the modelling framework presented here is capable of providing reliable information on treatment burden for presumed malaria at national and sub national scales.

the geostatistical modelling approach presented here provides, for the first time to our knowledge, a method for reliably quantifying the burden of disease at national and subnational scales using imperfect health management information system data.

the geostatistical model presented here provides reliable estimates of treatment burdens at any level of aggregation for any health facility that has reported data in the past, and can do so in the future.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we can now provide a complete picture of the treatment burden for presumed malaria in the Kenyan public health system.

the geostatistics approach presented here is a powerful tool to improve the use of imperfect data in health systems, and that it should be used to support the planning and monitoring processes in the public health arena.
we have demonstrated that it is possible to use imperfect data from HMIS in Kenya to provide accurate estimates of disease-specific treatment burdens at the national scale.
The main takeaway from our work is that
geostatistical methods can be used to improve HMIS data to the point that the information is useful for policy and planning.
the data from the HMIS can be used to generate accurate estimates of treatment burdens for presumed disease, but only if they are first corrected for underreporting.
the data available within HMIS are of sufficient quality to be used to define disease-specific treatment burdens at the district and provincial scale.
